newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown goes to Brussels to usher in new EU era.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown goes to Brussels to usher in new EU era.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will attend his first meeting of European Union finance ministers in Brussels on Monday with all sides hopeful a new era of relations has begun.
Britain, retaining the right to opt out of a single currency as well as shunning swathes of EU legislation, had a reputation as the pariah of Europe under former prime minister John Major.

But the early days of the Labour government suggests a new approach. "It is our commitment that we will draw a line under the sterile, negative and fruitless confrontation...of the previous British government," Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Wednesday, pledging a fresh start.

Economists said Labour will at least open up dialogue over a range of issues, even though the new government is unlikely to join the first wave of a single European currency in 1999 and will not budge on areas like control of borders and a common defence policy.
"What we've got now is the opportunity for dialogue and negotiation rather than a closed door," said Paul Horne, chief international economist at Smith Barney in Paris.

June's EU InterGovernmental Conference summit in Amsterdam now stood a much better chance of moving forward, he said. "The IGC has been totally obstructed by the Conservatives since last year. Now there is a chance for progress on expansion (of the EU), reform of the institutions and other issues."

Graham Bishop, adviser on European financial affairs at Salomon Brothers, said Labour's more pragmatic approach to qualified majority voting, allowing its extension where it suited Britain, would also be welcome.
As for Monday's meeting, EU officials are hoping for more of the same from Brown but only because his predecessor, Kenneth Clarke, was the most europhile member of a sceptical government.
"I must say it is no secret that Kenneth Clarke has been extremely constructive in the work of EU finance ministers", one senior EU official said.
None the less, Brown, with no election to worry about or hundreds of eurosceptics in his own party to appease, has the chance to achieve much more.

Bishop said a key test for Brown would be his willingness to allow progress on legal issues for the euro, such as its legal name and the continuity of financial contracts under European economic and monetary union (EMU).

EU leaders intended to put these issues into a legal text using Article 235 of the Maastricht treaty. But because it required unanimity, it was held up by Britain's Conservative government, wary of any EMU issue in the run up to elections.
"The City is pushing for the continuity of contracts to be cleared up and I can't see why Brown would want to delay long," Bishop said. "It will be a good test of his resolve."
The pace at which Labour has hit the ground running certainly suggests a new era at home and within the EU.

On Monday, just four days into government, Labour's new Europe minister, Doug Henderson, flew to Brussels to set the wheels in motion for Britain to sign the Social Chapter which guarantees certain minimum employment rights.
The Major government had steadfastly refused to sign the protocol, saying it would cost thousands of jobs.
The next day, Brown stunned the financial markets by granting the Bank of England operational independence to set interest rates for the first time in 300 years.

The Maastricht Treaty stipulates an independent central bank is a key prerequisite for EMU membership. Brown kept the right to override the Bank in exceptional circumstances and said the reforms were not made with EMU in mind.
But it would take only one more step to meet that Maastricht demand. "This is a building block, a launch pad," Bishop said. Not all EU leaders were happy with Labour's opening shots, however.

"The closed approach on some points...like common defence and security policy, the European justice system and internal affairs of the union are not very encouraging," Italian foreign minister Lamberto Dini said on Thursday.
Nonetheless, most commentators agreed the new broom that has swept through British politics will help not hinder the EU.

"The Germans and French really do want the pragmatic British point of view within the EU," Horne said. "They represent a very different view of economic and labour market issues and we all need that sort of triangular approach to the key issues."
But Britain is far from the centre of attention in the short-term. The spotlight rests firmly on France.

With elections due on May 25 and June 1 and France's pro-EMU centre-right neck-and-neck with the more sceptical Socialists, EMU's future is in the balance. "Britain's new stance is good news but all of this is academic until June 1," Horne said.
